source.title: Representational Alignment Supports Effective Machine Teaching
source.authors: Ilia Sucholutsky; Katherine M. Collins; Maya Malaviya; Nori Jacoby; Weiyang Liu; T. Sumers; Michalis Korakakis; Umang Bhatt; Mark K. Ho; J. B. Tenenbaum; B. Love; Z. Pardos; Adrian Weller; Thomas L. Griffiths

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study uses representational alignment as a framework and a controlled teaching-task variable, but it does not test whether independently trained models become more similar with scale or test any listed version of that claim.
record.gate_note: The study measures teacher-student alignment in a pedagogical task and reports its association with student learning. This is a related but different construct from convergence among independently trained models. Those results are recorded with versions ["none"] and described in fits_no_version. GRADE-Match comparisons are omitted because they report the performance of the study's proposed matching procedure, not what alignment itself does.
record.test_reason: The study builds a grid task (GRADE) where teacher-student 'representational alignment' is set by the experimenters through stimulus swaps, and measures how it affects student learning. It never measures alignment between independently trained models, across scale, modalities or seeds. It does not map between model representations or look for shared features. It also does not use the convergence finding as a tool. The convergence literature enters only as a general framing. So the study is T6, not T4.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is correct. The authors also state that machine teachers should be designed for representational alignment with human learners, not only for accuracy. They also propose GRADE-Match, which beats random assignment and MOOC-style assignment in simulation but does not reach the optimal assignment.
record.recipe_differences: GRADE measures teacher-student alignment using grid locations and Euclidean distance between pairwise swaps, and studies teaching outcomes; it does not use the original sources' tests of representation convergence across models or scale.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported relationship varies by stimulus set and category structure; the authors note that high-alignment ordering is less clear in column conditions.

fits_no_version.finding: In the human experiments, machine-teacher alignment with the student correlates with mean student accuracy, with r ranging from 0.52 to 0.91 depending on stimulus set and category structure. Several of these correlations are non-significant.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Teacher–student representational alignment, manipulated experimentally, improves learning outcomes in a controlled teaching task.

fits_no_version.finding: In simulations and in post-hoc analyses of the human data, higher alignment generally yields higher student accuracy at a fixed teacher error rate. The ordering is less clear at high alignment in the column conditions.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Alignment and teacher expertise jointly determine student learning, and high alignment can offset teacher error.

fits_no_version.finding: With student-centric teachers, accuracy falls rapidly as class size grows, then plateaus.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Class size and representational diversity moderate the benefit of aligning with students.

record.code_released: not stated; the paper says implementations will be made open-source upon publication
record.problems: The paper states that simulated students are always 1-NN classifiers and that their representations are fixed. The human experiments used 20 participants per condition; teacher-error effects for those experiments were simulated post hoc rather than tested with human participants. Several outcome values are presented only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted GRADE-Match versus random, MOOC/Min Err, and optimal-assignment outcome comparisons (Figure 1H; Tables 2–5), because they evaluate the proposed matching procedure rather than directly report what representational alignment itself does. Also omitted additional matching and grouping results in Appendix Figures 5 and Tables 2–5 for the same reason.

untested.parts: All of it: no models compared across scale, architecture, objective or data.
All of it: no vision–language representation comparison.
All of it: no networks trained from different initializations.
All of it: no mapping, stitching or relative representations.
All of it: no feature or circuit comparison across models.
All of it: no comparison of similarity metrics or input sets for model convergence.
All of it: no test of model-to-model alignment levels or their causes.

record.verdict_notes: The study shares the vocabulary of representational alignment but studies a different construct: experimenter-manipulated grid permutations between a teacher and a student, which are 1-NN agents or humans. Its rows are correctly linked to 'none'. The relation and tranche should be changed from uses_without_test/T4 to cites_only/T6, because the convergence finding plays no role in the method. Omitting the GRADE-Match rows is appropriate.

versions.untested_parts: No comparison of representation alignment across model scale, capability, architecture, objectives, or training data.
No vision-language model comparison or paired image-caption representation alignment.
No comparison of independently initialized networks or their shared features/subspaces.
No mapping, stitching, relative-representation, or unpaired alignment test between models.
No test for recurring interpretable features or circuits across models.
No comparison of convergence metrics, metric settings, input datasets, or out-of-distribution inputs.
No test of whether model alignment is incomplete or explained by shared training data or objectives.

rows.subject: simple 1-NN agents
rows.operation_detail: Measured student accuracy across teacher error rates and teacher-student grid alignment in the simple-features simulation.
rows.measure: Student classification accuracy as a function of teacher error rate and representational alignment
rows.value: The text states that for a fixed teacher error rate, higher representational alignment is always better, provided the error rate is not too high; numerical values are figure only.
rows.note: The result concerns alignment in a controlled teaching task, not convergence between independently trained models.
rows.check: The 'observed' state refers to the study's own alignment-to-accuracy hypothesis, not to any claim version. The same holds for the states of R2–R11.
